extracted.intended_audience: general readers, Twitch users, streamers, and researchers interested in Twitch platform policies and history
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of Twitch's platform rules, content-moderation policies, partner/affiliate monetization programs, and technical restrictions for broadcasters and viewers. Covers eligibility criteria, prohibited content, copyright handling, revenue-share tiers, and mitigation tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age restriction (Terms of Service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch's Terms of Service does not allow people under 13 years of age to use its services. Additionally, people who are at least 13 years old but below the age of majority in their jurisdiction may only use the services under the supervision or permission of a parent or other legal guardian who agrees to abide to the Terms of Service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner Program subscription revenue split and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Partner Program allows popular content producers to share in advertisement revenue and accept paid subscriptions (US$4.99 a month). Twitch retains US$2.49 of every US$4.99 channel subscription, with the remaining US$2.50 going directly to the partnered streamer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, Twitch previously required prospective partners have an 'average concurrent viewership of 500+' and a consistent streaming schedule of at least three days a week (exceptions were made). The 'Achievements' feature later provided a clearer 'Path to Partnership' with trackable goals for viewership, duration and frequency of streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliate Program eligibility and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliate Program (launched April 2017) allows smaller channels to generate revenue and access multi-priced subscription tiers. Participants get some but not all Partner benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliates can make profit from cheering with Bits, access Twitch Subscriptions (with a maximum of five subscriber emotes), and—since September 2019—receive a share of ad revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner Plus / Plus Program qualification and point system
rubrics_metrics.description: Partner Plus Program (introduced June 2023) recognizes Twitch partners who consistently bring a large audience and engagement. Streamers in this program receive a 70/30 revenue share on subscription revenue. To qualify originally, creators had to maintain a sub count of at least 350 subscribers for three consecutive months and qualifying members were enrolled for the next 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program uses a points system where each monthly subscription contributes points (one tier 1 subscription = 1 point, tier 2 = 2 points, tier 3 = 6 points). To qualify for the 60/40 revenue split, streamers must maintain 100 Plus Points for three consecutive months. For the 70/30 revenue split, streamers must maintain 300 Plus Points. In January 2024 Twitch added a 60/40 tier with lower requirements, expanded access to affiliates, and eliminated the $100,000 cap on the 70/30 split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity contract streaming-hour expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Streaming-hour requirements differ across exclusivity deals; reported examples: YouTube's contracts start at 100 hours of streaming time per month while Twitch's start at 200.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hour requirements affect streamers' work–life balance and are factors when streamers consider platform exclusivity offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic fingerprinting for copyrighted music (VODs)
rubrics_metrics.description: On-demand videos on Twitch are subject to acoustic fingerprinting using Audible Magic; if copyrighted music is detected, the 30-minute portion of the video which contains the music will be muted. Live broadcasts were not subject to these filters (at the time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitch provided a system to challenge incorrect matches and offered a selection of royalty-free music for streamers to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA takedown compliance and VOD/clip handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch complies with DMCA takedown notices; in June 2020 it issued takedowns and copyright strikes aimed at VODs and clips containing copyrighted music from prior years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamers were advised to remove VODs and clips if uncertain they contained copyrighted material; the enforcement sparked backlash due to loss of prior content and inability to rapidly review or delete content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundtrack extension: rights-cleared music in separate track
rubrics_metrics.description: Soundtrack (introduced Sept 2020) plays rights-cleared music with curated playlists in a separate audio track that is not recorded with VODs, and launched with agreements with multiple music distributors and independent labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was intended to address music-related takedowns, though some performance-rights organizations accused Twitch of designing Soundtrack to avoid certain licenses (mechanical and synchronization).

rubrics_metrics.name: DJ program constraints and royalty handling
rubrics_metrics.description: DJ program (introduced Sept 2024) allows DJs access to a DJ mixes stream category where music from participating labels may be streamed without DMCA risk, with a share of revenue used to pay royalties (deducted from affiliates'/partners' existing split).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program limitations: VODs and clips are disabled on enrolled channels (even if streaming non‑DJ content)—Twitch recommends using a separate account for non‑DJ streams. DJs are restricted to music from labels/publishers that have reached agreements, potentially restricting unofficial remixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on streaming 'Adults Only' (AO) and overt sexual or gratuitous violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch users are not allowed to stream any game rated 'Adults Only' (AO) by the ESRB in the United States, and any game that contains 'overtly sexual content' or 'gratuitous violence', or content which violates the terms of use of third-party services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly banned games regardless of rating
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch has explicitly banned specific games from streaming regardless of rating; examples include BMX XXX, eroge visual novels (such as Dramatical Murder), HuniePop, Rinse and Repeat, Second Life, and Yandere Simulator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bans may be applied even when similar games remain allowed, and have provoked developer complaints about arbitrary enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to coordinated misuse of game categories (Artifact example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When channels hijacked the Artifact category for off‑topic or inappropriate content (full copyrighted movies, pornography, extremist material, etc.), Twitch deleted offending accounts and temporarily banned new accounts from streaming until issue resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that Twitch may take broad temporary platform actions (deleting accounts, blocking new streams) when sections are overwhelmed by abusive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on 'sexually suggestive' non-nude content (Pools/Hot Tubs/Beaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch considered streams from hot tubs/swimsuit content as 'not advertiser friendly' and applied bans/enforcements; in May 2021 Twitch clarified its 'Pools, Hot Tubs, and Beaches' policy as targeting content it deemed 'sexually suggestive' rather than discriminating against specific genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar actions were applied to yoga+ASMR streams deemed to be approaching sexual content. Policy enforcement is based on 'sexually suggestive' determinations rather than simple context like swimsuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual content policy revisions and rescindment (Dec 2023)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Dec 2023 Twitch introduced a policy relaxing prohibitions on certain adult content if appropriately labeled (including allowing depictions of 'fictionalized nudity'), but rescinded the policy shortly after due to backlash and removed content that violated the update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following backlash, Twitch reversed course: will no longer permit depictions of real or fictional nudity, regardless of medium. Some prior allowances (highlighting certain body parts and specific dances without a label) remained in effect, while games featuring nudity or sexual violence continue to be prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech and harassment policy (sliding scale of remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch updated acceptable content policies (Feb 2018) to remove hateful content and in Dec 2020 announced a new harassment and hateful content policy effective Jan 22, 2021, with a more strict stance and a larger sliding scale of remedies (temporary blocks, full bans, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New rules included banning imagery containing the Confederate Flag and 'racist emotes' and banning words considered sexual insults (e.g., 'incel', 'virgin', 'simp') when used for harassment. Twitch clarified penalties only apply when such terms are used to harass others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible labeling change: removal of 'blind playthrough' tag
rubrics_metrics.description: On Dec 4, 2020 Twitch removed the 'blind playthrough' tag due to concerns of ableism that it may be offensive to those who are visually impaired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested non-offensive alternatives include 'first playthrough', 'undiscovered', and 'no spoilers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Raid feature and hate-raid mitigations (chat participation limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitch supports 'raids' (sending viewers to another channel) as a growth tool. In mid-2021 large-scale 'hate raids' began where bots flooded chats with harassment. Twitch introduced mitigation tools allowing streamers to limit chat participation to users who verified phone or email with Twitch, or to those who have followed the channel for a minimum amount of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools are intended to reduce bot-driven harassment and give streamers control over chat access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling streaming restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: On Sept 20, 2022 Twitch announced it would prohibit streaming of slots, roulette and dice games on gambling websites not licensed in the US or 'other jurisdictions that provide sufficient consumer protection'. The policy change does not affect sports betting, fantasy sports, and poker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This targets gambling-centric content from unregulated operators; streamers sponsored by online gambling services and the broader popularity/controversy of gambling streams are context for the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform support and broadcasting sources (technical interoperability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users can watch Twitch via web browser and dedicated apps on Android, Fire OS, iOS, TV platforms (Fire TV, webOS, Samsung TVs (2020+), Android TV, Apple TV), and consoles (PS4/PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S). Broadcasters can stream from various platforms (mobile apps, OBS Studio, Twitch Studio, native console integrations, third‑party apps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some platform apps (e.g., older console apps, Twitch Desktop App) have been deprecated or had features removed; broadcasting/feature availability varies by platform and over time.
